paras.t: Impii autem, præsertim qui peccant ex habitu pravo, manibus et verbis, id est factis ac dictis, accessierunt illam, id est, injustitiam seu mortem culpæ advocaverunt, et accesserunt. De quibus in libro Job fertur, quod quasi de industria recesserunt a Deo. Excogitant etenim et laborant, qualiter impiam inclinationem opere exsequantur. Et existimantes illam amicam, id est, tanquam rem caram et congruentem sibi, apprehendentes eam propter delectationem annexam, aut propter alium finem perversum, defluxerunt, id est, per diversa vitia sunt dispersi. Talium quippe judicium est ita corruptum, quod malum sub ratione boni concipiunt, et lætantur quum impie egerint, quia ex habitu vitioso sic inclinantur. Ideo ait Philosophus: Qualis quisque est, talis sibi finis bonus videtur ac placet. Et Salomon: Via, inquit, stulti recta in oculis ejus. Et sponsiones posuerunt ad illam, id est, firmiter statuerunt adhærere iniquitati, quemadmodum sponsus sponsæ. De quibus in Zacharia legitur: Cor suum posuerunt ut adamantem, ne audirent legem. Et Jeremias: Induraverunt, inquit, facies suas supra petram, et noluerunt reverti. Quibus in Isaia ait sermo divinus: Dixistis: Percussimus fœdus cum morte, et cum inferno fecimus pactum. Hoc etenim dicunt ipso facto, quamvis non verbo. Quoniam morte æternæ damnationis digni sunt, qui sunt ex parte illius, utpote injustitiæ, hoc est injusti injustitiæ servi. Juxta quod dicitur Deo in Psalmo: Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem; et, Neque permanebunt injusti ante oculos tuos.
paras.en: [[1:16|But the wicked|Impii autem]], especially those who sin from an evil habit, [[1:16|with works and words|manibus et verbis]] [literally "with hands and words"], that is, by deeds and sayings, [[1:16|have called it to them|accessierunt illam]], that is, have summoned injustice, or the death of guilt, and have drawn near to it [Denis's text reads *accessierunt*, and he glosses it both as "have summoned" (*accersierunt*, the Vulgate's word) and as "have drawn near" (*accesserunt*)]. Of such it is said in the book of Job that they [[Job 34:27|as it were on purpose have revolted|quasi de industria recesserunt]] from God. For they devise and labour how they may carry out their wicked inclination in deed. [[1:16|and esteeming it a friend|Et existimantes illam amicam]], that is, as a thing dear and fitting to themselves, laying hold of it for the delight joined to it, or for some other perverse end, [[1:16|have fallen away|defluxerunt]] [literally "have flowed away"], that is, have been scattered through divers vices. For the judgment of such men is so corrupted that they conceive evil under the aspect of good, and [[Prov 2:14|are glad when they have done evil|lætantur quum impie egerint]], because they are so inclined by a vicious habit. Therefore the Philosopher says: As each man is, such does the end seem good and pleasing to him. And Solomon: [[Prov 12:15|The way|Via]], he says, [[Prov 12:15|of a fool is right in his own eyes|stulti recta in oculis ejus]]. [[1:16|and have made a covenant with it|Et sponsiones posuerunt ad illam]] [literally "have made pledges to it", as of betrothal], that is, have firmly resolved to cleave to iniquity, as a bridegroom to his bride. Of whom we read in Zacharias: [[Zach 7:12|they made their heart as the adamant stone, lest they should hear the law|Cor suum posuerunt ut adamantem, ne audirent legem]]. And Jeremias: [[Jer 5:3|they have made their faces harder than the rock, and they have refused to return|Induraverunt, inquit, facies suas supra petram, et noluerunt reverti]]. To whom the divine word says in Isaias: [[Is 28:15|you have said: We have entered into a league with death, and we have made a covenant with hell|Dixistis: Percussimus fœdus cum morte, et cum inferno fecimus pactum]]. For this they say by the very deed, though not in word. [[1:16|because|Quoniam]] [[1:16|they are worthy|digni sunt]] of the death of eternal damnation, [[1:16|to be of the part thereof|qui sunt ex parte illius]] [Denis reads "who are of its part"], namely of injustice, that is, the unjust, the slaves of injustice. According to what is said to God in the Psalm: [[Ps 5:7|Thou hatest all the workers of iniquity|Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem]]; and: [[Ps 5:6|nor shall the unjust abide before thy eyes|Neque permanebunt injusti ante oculos tuos]].

2.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI SECUNDI : DIXERUNT IMPII, COGITANTES APUD SE NON RECTE.
2.title_en: Explanation of the second chapter: The wicked have said, reasoning with themselves, but not right

paras.t: Ut opposita juxta se posita evidentius innotescant, auctor hujus voluminis, præmisso uno capitulo documenta sapientialia continente, et infra de sapientia plenius tractaturus, interponit hic unum capitulum de insipientium erroribus ac peccatis, dicens:
paras.en: That opposites set side by side may be the more plainly seen, the author of this book, having first set down one chapter containing teachings of wisdom, and being about to treat of wisdom more fully further on, here puts in between one chapter on the errors and sins of the unwise, saying:

paras.t: Dixerunt impii, cogitantes apud se non recte, id est, ex perversa et perfida cogitatione locuti sunt verba infidelia et mendosa: quia ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, et ea quæ sunt in voce, sunt signa et notæ conceptionum affectionumque animæ. Ideo qualis vir, talis sermo. Exiguum et cum tædio est tempus vitæ nostræ, id est breve, et tædiis afflictionibusque admixtum: sicut et sanctus Job loquitur, Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis; Paulus quoque, Quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ. Et non est refrigerium in fine hominis, id est quies et merces post mortem, nec tempore mortis restat spes vitæ alterius. Juxta quod ex persona talium dicitur perfidorum in Ecclesiaste: Unus est interitus hominis et jumentorum, et æqua utriusque conditio; et nihil habet homo jumento amplius. Et rursus Scriptura ait: Comedamus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur. Et non est qui agnitus sit reversus ab inferis. Quasi dicant: Nil certi scitur de alia vita. Hoc impii isti faciliter sibi persuadent, non considerantes historias sacræ Scripturæ, Sanctorum legendas, in quibus multi resuscitati leguntur, imo et aliqui in mortalibus defuncti, et pœnas purgatorii ac inferni experti: qui reversi, narraverunt viventibus quæ viderunt atque senserunt.
paras.en: The wicked [[2:1|have said, reasoning with themselves, but not right|Dixerunt impii, cogitantes apud se non recte]] [Denis reads *Dixerunt impii*, "the wicked have said", where the Vulgate has *Dixerunt enim*, "for they have said"]: that is, out of perverse and faithless thinking they spoke faithless and lying words: for [[Matt 12:34|out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh|ex abundantia cordis os loquitur]], and the things that are in the voice are signs and tokens of the conceptions and affections of the soul. Therefore as the man is, so is his speech. [[2:1|The time of our life is short and tedious|Exiguum et cum tædio est tempus vitæ nostræ]], that is, brief, and mingled with weariness and afflictions: as holy Job also says, [[Job 14:1|Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries|Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis]]; and Paul too: [[2 Cor 4:17|that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation|Quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ]]. [[2:1|and in the end of a man there is no remedy|Et non est refrigerium in fine hominis]] [*refrigerium*, literally "refreshment"], that is, no rest and reward after death, nor at the time of death does there remain any hope of another life. In accordance with which it is said in Ecclesiastes in the person of such faithless men: [[Eccles 3:19|the death of man, and of beasts is one, and the condition of them both is equal|Unus est interitus hominis et jumentorum, et æqua utriusque conditio]]; and [[Eccles 3:19|man hath nothing more than beast|nihil habet homo jumento amplius]]. And again the Scripture says: [[Is 22:13|Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die|Comedamus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur]]. [[2:1|and no man hath been known to have returned from hell|Et non est qui agnitus sit reversus ab inferis]]. As if they said: Nothing certain is known of another life. Of this these wicked men readily persuade themselves, not considering the histories of holy Scripture and the legends of the Saints, in which we read of many raised from the dead, and indeed of some who died in mortal sins and experienced the pains of purgatory and of hell, who, having returned, told the living what they had seen and felt.

paras.t: Quia ex nihilo nati sumus, quantum ad animam, et quoad ipsam materiam primam in exordio temporis ex nihilo factam, secundum quod ponuntur quatuor coæquæva, videlicet tempus, cœlum, angelus, materia: de quibus in libro de IV Coæquævis diffuse tractat Albertus. Unde et Deus vocatur Conditor omnium rerum. Hæc autem particula refertur ad illam, Non est refrigerium in fine hominis. Tanquam dicant: Sicut ex nihilo facti sumus, ita post mortem nihil nostri manebit. Hinc subditur: et post hæc erimus tanquam si non fuerimus: quoniam fumus afflatus, id est aer instar fumi spiratus, est in naribus nostris: quoniam inspirando respirandoque vivimus; et sermo scintillæ ad commovendum cor nostrum, id est calor naturalis, modicus ut scintilla, et sermone significatus: cujus caloris virtute cor se movet, et membris influit motum. Et sumitur hic Cor, pro parte corporea quæ dicitur fons caloris, et primum vivens, ac ultimo moriens in animali, secundum Philosophum.
paras.en: [[2:2|For we are born of nothing|Quia ex nihilo nati sumus]]: as to the soul, and as to prime matter itself, made out of nothing at the beginning of time; according to which four things are held to be coeval [that is, created together at the first instant], namely time, heaven, the angel and matter, of which Albert treats at length in the book *On the Four Coevals*. Hence God is also called the Maker of all things. Now this phrase is referred to that other one, [[2:1|in the end of a man there is no remedy|Non est refrigerium in fine hominis]]; as though they said: As we were made out of nothing, so after death nothing of us will remain. Hence it is added: [[2:2|and after this we shall be as if we had not been|et post hæc erimus tanquam si non fuerimus]]: [[2:2|for the breath|quoniam fumus afflatus]], that is, the air breathed out like smoke, [[2:2|in our nostrils is smoke|est in naribus nostris]]: since we live by breathing in and breathing out; [[2:2|and speech a spark to move our heart|et sermo scintillæ ad commovendum cor nostrum]], that is, the natural heat, small as a spark, and signified by *speech*, by the power of which heat the heart moves itself and pours motion into the members. And *heart* is taken here for the bodily part which is called the source of heat, and the first thing living and the last dying in an animal, according to the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle].

paras.t: Quia extinctus cinis erit corpus nostrum. Post mortem enim corpus exanime incineratur. Et spiritus diffundetur tanquam mollis aer, id est, spiritus animales et vitales ac motivi deficient. Vel Spiritus diffundetur, id est, in nihilum resolvetur ac evanesceret, sicut mollis aer, qui a suo contrario fugatur, ac cito corrumpitur. Et transibit vita nostra, id est, suo cursu deficiet, tanquam vestigium nubis, quæ cito dissolvitur. Unde subjungitur: et sicut nebula dissolvetur, quæ nebula fugata est a radiis solis, et a calore illius aggravata, id est victa, dispersa, seu pressa deorsum calore radiorum solarium, tempore magni æstus, quo raro pluit, sicut et tempore frigoris maximi. Intentus equidem calor vapores nubis dissolvit sive consumit; vehemens vero frigus eos constringit.
paras.en: [[2:3|Which being put out, our body shall be ashes|Quia extinctus cinis erit corpus nostrum]] [Denis reads *Quia extinctus*, "for, put out, our body …", for the Vulgate's *qua extincta*]. For after death the lifeless body is turned to ashes. [[2:3|and our spirit shall be poured abroad as soft air|Et spiritus diffundetur tanquam mollis aer]], that is, the animal, vital and motive spirits [in the physiology of the time, the subtle vapours that carry sensation, life and movement through the body] will fail. Or, *the spirit shall be poured abroad*, that is, it will be dissolved into nothing and vanish, like soft air, which is driven away by its contrary and is quickly corrupted. [[2:3|And our life shall pass away|Et transibit vita nostra]], that is, will fail in its course, [[2:3|as the trace of a cloud|tanquam vestigium nubis]], which is quickly dissolved. Hence it is added: [[2:3|and shall be dispersed as a mist, which is driven away by the beams of the sun, and overpowered with the heat thereof|et sicut nebula dissolvetur, quæ nebula fugata est a radiis solis, et a calore illius aggravata]], that is, overcome, scattered, or pressed down by the heat of the sun's rays in a time of great heat, when it seldom rains, as also in a time of the greatest cold. For intense heat dissolves or consumes the vapours of the cloud, while fierce cold binds them together.

paras.t: Et nomen nostrum oblivionem accipiet per tempus, id est, paulatim deficiet memoria personæ ac nominis nostri: juxta illud, Futura tempora oblivione cuncta operient. Verumtamen, sicut aliqui ob actuum suorum laudabilem eminentiam, relinquunt post se perpetuam sui memoriam; ita nonnulli propter præcipuam suam perversitatem, manent in perpetua quadam hominum memoria cum vituperiis: juxta quod in Proverbiis scriptum est, Memoria justi cum laude, nomen impiorum putrescet. Et nemo memoriam habebit operum nostrorum: prout in Ecclesiaste habetur: Non est priorum memoria; sed nec eorum quidem quæ postea futura sunt, erit recordatio apud eos qui futuri sunt in novissimo.
paras.en: [[2:4|And our name in time shall be forgotten|Et nomen nostrum oblivionem accipiet per tempus]], that is, little by little the memory of our person and of our name will fail: according to that saying, [[Eccles 2:16|the times to come shall cover all things together with oblivion|Futura tempora oblivione cuncta operient]]. Yet, as some through the praiseworthy excellence of their deeds leave behind them an everlasting memory of themselves, so some, for their exceptional wickedness, remain in a kind of lasting memory among men, with reproach: according to what is written in Proverbs, [[Prov 10:7|The memory of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot|Memoria justi cum laude, nomen impiorum putrescet]]. [[2:4|and no man shall have any remembrance of our works|Et nemo memoriam habebit operum nostrorum]]: as is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:11|There is no remembrance of former things: nor indeed of those things which hereafter are to come, shall there be any remembrance with them that shall be in the latter end|Non est priorum memoria; sed nec eorum quidem quæ postea futura sunt, erit recordatio apud eos qui futuri sunt in novissimo]].

paras.t: Umbræ enim transitus est tempus nostrum: id est, duratio vitæ nostræ, brevis ac defluens est, sicut apparentia umbræ: quæ secundum motum ambulantis videtur procedere, et celerrime evanescit. Unde et primo Paralipomenon habetur: Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora; et in Psalmo, Quia defecerunt sicut fumus dies mei. Et non est reversio finis nostri: id est, post mortem non revertemur ad vitam hanc: sicut et sanctus Job, Viam, inquit, per quam non revertar, ambulo. Quoniam consignata est, id est clausa, operta, et nunquam apparens, quia nec exsistens ipsa reversio. Sicque per molem sepulcro superimpositam est sublata: quemadmodum et Judæi, corpore Christi clauso in monumento per lapidem consignatum, putabant ejus memoriam, omnemque spem suæ resurrectionis, esse penitus exstinguendas. Unde et in Psalmo: Sepulcra eorum, domus illorum in æternum. Et nemo revertetur ad hanc vitam post mortem. Quod quamvis naturaliter ita sit, miraculose tamen frequenter contingit oppositum.
paras.en: [[2:5|For our time is as the passing of a shadow|Umbræ enim transitus est tempus nostrum]]: that is, the length of our life is short and flowing away, like the appearance of a shadow, which seems to go forward with the movement of one walking, and vanishes very quickly. Hence it is said in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]] [the margin gives Par. xxix, 5; the words are in v. 15]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 101:4|For my days are vanished like smoke|Quia defecerunt sicut fumus dies mei]]. [[2:5|And there is no going back of our end|Et non est reversio finis nostri]]: that is, after death we shall not return to this life: as holy Job also says: [[Job 16:23|a path|Viam]], he says, [[Job 16:23|by which I shall not return|per quam non revertar]], [[Job 16:23|I am walking|ambulo]]. [[2:5|For it is fast sealed|Quoniam consignata est]], that is, shut, covered, and never appearing, because the return itself does not even exist. And so it has been taken away by the mass laid upon the tomb: just as the Jews, when the body of Christ was shut in the sepulchre by a sealed stone, thought that his memory, and all hope of his resurrection, must be utterly extinguished[[Matt 27:64||]][[Matt 27:66||]]. Hence also in the Psalm: [[Ps 48:12|their sepulchres shall be their houses for ever|Sepulcra eorum, domus illorum in æternum]]. [[2:5|And no man returneth|Et nemo revertetur]] to this life after death. And though by nature it is so, yet by miracle the opposite often happens.

paras.t: Venite ergo, et fruamur bonis quæ sunt: id est, quum non sit vita alia post præsentem, nec retributio, imo nec tandem memoria, non quæramus nisi delectabilia carni, et desiderabilia hujus mundi. Quidam autem quamvis non crederent esse vitam post istam, tamen desiderio magnæ famæ, qua in memoriis hominum remanerent, studuerunt agere quædam bona et magna. Isti vero considerantes famam quoque tandem deficere, toto impetu elegerunt vacare libidini: quemadmodum in Ecclesiaste ex persona talium legitur: Comede in lætitia panem tuum, et bibe cum jucunditate vinum tuum; perfruere vita cum uxore quam diligis: hæc est enim pars tua. Et utamur creatura tanquam in juventute celeriter, id est, rebus creatis ad libitum sine mora inhæreamus.
paras.en: [[2:6|Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that are present|Venite ergo, et fruamur bonis quæ sunt]]: that is, since there is no other life after the present one, nor any requital, nor even, in the end, any memory, let us seek nothing but what is pleasant to the flesh and desirable in this world. Some, indeed, though they did not believe there was a life after this one, yet out of desire for great fame, by which they might live on in the memory of men, strove to do certain good and great things. But these men, considering that fame too fails at last, chose with all their force to give themselves to lust: as we read in Ecclesiastes, in the person of such men: [[Eccles 9:7|eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with gladness|Comede in lætitia panem tuum, et bibe cum jucunditate vinum tuum]]; [[Eccles 9:9|Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest|perfruere vita cum uxore quam diligis]]: [[Eccles 9:9|for this is thy portion|hæc est enim pars tua]]. [[2:6|and let us speedily use the creatures as in youth|Et utamur creatura tanquam in juventute celeriter]], that is, let us cling to created things at our pleasure, without delay.

paras.t: Vino pretioso, quantum ad gustum, et unguentis, quoad tactum et odoratum, nos impleamus, quatenus singuli sensus nostri delectationibus utantur objectorum suorum; et non prætereat nos flos temporis: id est, adolescentiam, seu juventutem nostræ durationis, non expendamus absque abundantia voluptatum. Coronemus nos rosis antequam marcescant, ut sic ornati, mulieribus magis complaceamus; nullum pratum sit, quod non pertranseat luxuria nostra: id est, in locis virentibus et amœnis nostram exerceamus libidinem. Nemo vestrum exsors sit, id est sine communione et participatione, luxuriæ nostræ; ubique relinquamus signa lætitiæ: quoniam hæc est pars nostra, et hæc est sors nostra, id est, taliter delectari et vivere, est præcipuum bonum nostrum et eventus fortunatior qui potest nobis accidere, quia in his felicitatem constituimus nostram: juxta illud Ecclesiastæ, Quid amplius habet homo de labore suo?
paras.en: [[2:7|with costly wine|Vino pretioso]], as to taste, [[2:7|and ointments|et unguentis]], as to touch and smell, [[2:7|Let us fill ourselves|nos impleamus]], so that each of our senses may enjoy the delights of its own objects; [[2:7|and let not the flower of the time pass by us|et non prætereat nos flos temporis]]: that is, let us not spend the youth or prime of our span without an abundance of pleasures. [[2:8|Let us crown ourselves with roses, before they be withered|Coronemus nos rosis antequam marcescant]], so that, thus adorned, we may please women the more; [[2:8|let no meadow escape our riot|nullum pratum sit, quod non pertranseat luxuria nostra]]: that is, let us practise our lust in green and pleasant places. [[2:9|Let none of us go without his part|Nemo vestrum exsors sit]] [Denis's text reads *vestrum*, "of you", for the Vulgate's *nostrum*], that is, without fellowship and share, [[2:9|in luxury|luxuriæ nostræ]]; [[2:9|let us every where leave tokens of joy: for this is our portion, and this our lot|ubique relinquamus signa lætitiæ: quoniam hæc est pars nostra, et hæc est sors nostra]]: that is, so to take our pleasure and live is our chief good, and the happiest lot that can befall us, because we set our happiness in these things: according to that saying of Ecclesiastes, [[Eccles 3:9|What hath man more of his labour?|Quid amplius habet homo de labore suo?]]

paras.t: Præterea, quoniam vitia ista carnalia hominem in tantum exæcant, ut cadat in crudelitatem, et alios spoliet ut habeat unde suam explicat voluptatem; et præcipue eum exasperant contra eum a quo pro suis corripitur vitiis, recte subjungitur de impiis ista dicentibus: Opprimamus pauperem spiritu, id est humilem, justum, qui vel non possit, aut non optet nobis resistere; et non parcamus viduæ: quum tamen pauperes et viduæ sint miserabiles personæ, in quas exercere tyrannidem, est specialiter sævum; nec veterani revereamur canos multi temporis, id est, non honoremus senes, qui habent albos crines ex diuturnitate vitæ: quum tamen scriptum sit, Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis. Sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ, id est, potestate utamur pro jure, et voluntate pro ratione: quod proprium est tyrannis. Rex autem sequitur rationem, et potestatem regulat legibus æquitatis. Quod enim infirmum est, inutile invenitur: id est, inutile judicamus succumbere, impotentioremque esse, ac subjici; dominari vero et prævalere, reputamus beatum: quum tamen dicat Apostolus, Infirma mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia; et multo salubrius sit injurias pati, quam irrogare, Christo testante, Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, etc.
paras.en: Moreover, since these carnal vices so blind a man that he falls into cruelty, and plunders others so as to have the means to satisfy his pleasure; and since they especially embitter him against the one who rebukes him for his vices, it is rightly added of the wicked who say these things: [[2:10|Let us oppress the poor|Opprimamus pauperem]] in spirit, that is, the humble, [[2:10|just man|justum]], who either cannot or does not wish to resist us; [[2:10|and not spare the widow|et non parcamus viduæ]]: though the poor and widows are persons deserving pity, against whom to practise tyranny is especially savage; [[2:10|nor honour the ancient grey hairs of the aged|nec veterani revereamur canos multi temporis]], that is, let us not honour old men, who have white hair from length of life: though it is written, [[Lev 19:32|Rise up before the hoary head, and honour the person of the aged man|Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis]]. [[2:11|But let our strength be the law of justice|Sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ]], that is, let us use might for right, and will for reason, which is the mark of tyrants. A king, on the other hand, follows reason, and rules his power by the laws of equity. [[2:11|for that which is feeble is found to be nothing worth|Quod enim infirmum est, inutile invenitur]]: that is, we judge it worthless to give way, to be the weaker, and to be subject, but to rule and prevail we count blessed: though the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 1:27|the weak things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the strong|Infirma mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia]]; and it is far more wholesome to suffer wrongs than to inflict them, as Christ bears witness: [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]], etc.

paras.t: Porro quæ sequuntur, secundum Augustinum, verba sunt Salomonis, ad litteram de Christi passione et persecutione prænuntiata: et littera ad hoc optime consonat, nec de alio aliquo tam convenienter aptatur. Sed huic expositioni non videntur consonare præhabita: pontifices namque, Scribæ ac Pharisæi persecutores Christi, non fuerunt illius perfidiæ, ut dicerent animas hominum esse mortales; nec ad luxurias et cetera vitia jam prætacta totaliter se exposuerunt. Ad quod dici potest, quod inter illos fuerunt aliqui Sadducæi, qui animarum immortalitatem et futurum judicium negaverunt. Ceteri autem ita obtenebrati et carnales fuerunt, quod etsi non verbo, tamen ipso facto dixerunt, Venite, et fruamur bonis quæ sunt: quemadmodum de quibusdam scribit Apostolus, Dicunt se nosse Deum, factis autem negant. Fuerunt quippe summe avari, et præsentibus dediti. Propter quod Christum contra avaritiam prædicantem, atque terrenorum contemptum exemplo ac verbis persuadentem maxime abhorruerunt et irriserunt, dicentes: Dæmonium habet et insanit: quid eum auditis? prout in Evangelio legitur.
paras.en: Now what follows, according to Augustine, are words of Solomon foretelling, in the literal sense, the passion and persecution of Christ; and the letter agrees with this excellently, nor can it be fitted so aptly to anyone else. But what went before does not seem to agree with this exposition: for the chief priests, Scribes and Pharisees, the persecutors of Christ, were not of such unbelief as to say that the souls of men are mortal; nor did they give themselves over entirely to riot and the other vices already touched on. To this it can be said that among them were some Sadducees, who denied the immortality of souls and the judgment to come[[Acts 23:8||]]. The rest were so darkened and carnal that, if not in word, yet in very deed they said, [[2:6|Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that are present|Venite, et fruamur bonis quæ sunt]]: as the Apostle writes of certain men, [[Tit 1:16|They profess that they know God: but in their works they deny him|Dicunt se nosse Deum, factis autem negant]]. For they were exceedingly covetous, and given over to present things. For this reason, when Christ preached against avarice[[Luke 16:13||]], and urged the contempt of earthly things by example and by word, they abhorred him exceedingly and derided him[[Luke 16:14||]], saying: [[John 10:20|He hath a devil and is mad. Why hear you him?|Dæmonium habet et insanit: quid eum auditis?]] as we read in the Gospel.

paras.t: Exponendo ergo de Christo, iste est sensus: Circumveniamus ergo justum, id est, Jesum decipiamus: quia multas posuerunt ei insidias, et frequenter observaverunt, ac quosdam miserunt qui eum caperent in sermone. Et quamvis Jesus omnia sciens, non potuerit decipi, ipsi tamen præsumperunt se posse fallere eum, tanquam hominem purum aliis similem. Unde ait Salvator in Psalmo: Quoniam gratis absconderunt mihi interitum laquei sui; et denuo: Narraverunt ut absconderent laqueos; dixerunt, Quis videbit eos? Et quamvis dicatur hic ex eorum persona, Circumveniamus justum; ipsi tamen Jesum non reputaverunt nec nominaverunt justum. Sed quia verissime justus fuit, ideo ad rem ipsam adspiciendo dixerunt, Circumveniamus justum: quoniam is de quo sic contulerunt, fuit summe justus.
paras.en: Expounding it, then, of Christ, this is the sense: [[2:12|Let us, therefore, lie in wait for the just|Circumveniamus ergo justum]] [*circumvenire*, "to get round, to outwit"], that is, let us deceive Jesus: for they laid many snares for him, and often watched him[[John 8:6||]][[Mark 3:2||]][[Luke 14:1||]], and sent certain men to catch him in his speech[[Luke 20:20||]] [the margin gives John viii, 3–6; Mark iii, 2; Luke xiv, 1; xx, 20]. And though Jesus, knowing all things, could not be deceived, yet they presumed that they could deceive him, as a mere man like others. Hence the Saviour says in the Psalm: [[Ps 34:7|For without cause they have hidden their net for me unto destruction|Quoniam gratis absconderunt mihi interitum laquei sui]]; and again: [[Ps 63:6|They have talked of hiding snares; they have said: Who shall see them?|Narraverunt ut absconderent laqueos; dixerunt, Quis videbit eos?]] And though it is said here in their person, [[2:12|lie in wait for the just|Circumveniamus justum]], yet they themselves did not reckon Jesus just, nor call him so. But because he was most truly just, therefore, looking to the thing itself, they are made to say, *Let us lie in wait for the just*: since he about whom they so took counsel was supremely just.

paras.t: Sic et in Apocalypsi ministri Antichristi leguntur dicturi, Quis similis bestiæ? quum tamen dicturi sint, Quis similis Christo? Sed quoniam is quem pro Christo recipient, bestialissimus erit; ideo respiciendo ad rem, prænuntiantur dicturi, Quis similis bestiæ? Quoniam inutilis est nobis. Christus, quantum in se erat, utilissimus et saluberrimus fuit illis, eos erudiendo doctrinis, exemplis, miraculis, et caritative corripiendo ac advisando. Sed inutilis fuit eis, quoad perversum finem ab eis intentum: quoniam toto affectu inhiabant divitiis atque honoribus: quod Christus vituperavit, humilitatem et paupertatem exemplis ac verbis commendans. Juxta hunc modum narratur secundo Regum, quod consilium Achitophel utile fuit Absaloni ac suis: quod tamen sceleratissimum erat. Et contrarius est operibus nostris: quia opera ejus fuerunt sanctissima, opera autem ipsorum pravissima. Et improperat nobis peccata legis Mosaicæ, id est, imputat et objicit nobis peccata quæ contra legem Moysis perpetramus sive admittimus: prout in Evangelio copiose narratur; et diffamat in nos peccata disciplinæ nostræ, id est, publice reprehendit nos de statutis et observantiis quibusdam regularibus, asserens ea esse vitiosa ac divinæ legi contraria. Nempe in Evangelio ait: Bene irritum fecistis mandatum Dei propter traditionem vestram; et rursus, Quare vos transgredimini præceptum Dei, ut traditionem vestram servetis?
paras.en: So too in the Apocalypse the ministers of Antichrist are read as about to say, [[Apoc 13:4|Who is like to the beast|Quis similis bestiæ]]? though what they will say is, Who is like to Christ? But since he whom they will receive as Christ will be most beastly, therefore, looking to the thing, they are foretold as saying, [[Apoc 13:4|Who is like to the beast|Quis similis bestiæ]]? [[2:12|because he is not for our turn|Quoniam inutilis est nobis]] [*inutilis*, literally "useless, unprofitable"]. Christ, as far as lay in him, was most useful and most wholesome to them, instructing them by teaching, by example, by miracles, and by rebuking and admonishing them in charity. But he was useless to them as regards the perverse end they intended: for they gaped with all their desire after riches and honours, which Christ found fault with, commending humility and poverty by example and by word. In this manner it is told in the second book of Kings that the counsel of Achitophel was *profitable* to Absalom and his men[[2 Kings 17:14||]], though it was most wicked. [[2:12|and he is contrary to our doings|Et contrarius est operibus nostris]]: for his works were most holy, and theirs most depraved. [[2:12|and upbraideth us with transgressions of the law|Et improperat nobis peccata legis]] of Moses, that is, he charges and casts up to us the sins that we commit or allow against the law of Moses: as is told at length in the Gospel[[John 7:19||]]; [[2:12|and divulgeth against us the sins of our way of life|et diffamat in nos peccata disciplinæ nostræ]] [*disciplina*, "discipline, rule of life"], that is, he publicly rebukes us over certain statutes and regular observances, declaring them to be faulty and contrary to the divine law. For in the Gospel he says: [[Mark 7:9|Well do you make void the commandment of God|Bene irritum fecistis mandatum Dei]] [[Matt 15:6|for your tradition|propter traditionem vestram]]; and again: [[Matt 15:3|Why do you also transgress the commandment of God|Quare vos transgredimini præceptum Dei]], [[Mark 7:9|that you may keep your own tradition|ut traditionem vestram servetis]]? [Denis joins the words of Matt 15:3, 6 and Mark 7:9]

paras.t: Promittit, id est, firmiter asserit, se scientiam Dei habere, imo et Deo Patri in scientia esse æqualem, dicens: Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater; neque Patrem quis novit, nisi Filius. Et alibi: Mea doctrina non est mea, sed ejus qui misit me. Et iterum ad Judæos ibidem: Est verus qui misit me, quem vos nescitis: ego autem scio eum; et si dixero quia nescio eum, ero similis vobis, mendax. Et Filium Dei se nominat, imo Filium naturalem unigenitum consubstantialem, dicendo: Ego et Pater unum sumus; et rursus, Pater quod dedit mihi, majus omnibus est. Unde rursus apud Joannem habetur: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Propterea persequebantur Judæi Jesum, quia non solum solvebat sabbatum, sed et patrem suum dicebat Deum, æqualem se faciens Deo. Et alibi: Quem Pater sanctificavit, et misit in mundum, vos dicitis, Quia blasphemas: quia dixi, Filius Dei sum?
paras.en: [[2:13|He boasteth|Promittit]] [*promittit*, literally "he promises", which Denis takes as "he declares"], that is, he firmly asserts, [[2:13|that he hath the knowledge of God|se scientiam Dei habere]], and indeed that he is equal in knowledge to God the Father, saying: [[Matt 11:27|no one knoweth the Son but the Father: neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son|Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater; neque Patrem quis novit, nisi Filius]]. And elsewhere: [[John 7:16|My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me|Mea doctrina non est mea, sed ejus qui misit me]]. And again, to the Jews in the same place: [[John 7:28|he that sent me is true, whom you know not|Est verus qui misit me, quem vos nescitis]]: [[John 7:29|I know him|ego autem scio eum]]; [[John 8:55|And if I shall say that I know him not, I shall be like to you, a liar|et si dixero quia nescio eum, ero similis vobis, mendax]] [Denis joins John 7:28–29 with the end of John 8:55]. [[2:13|and calleth himself the son of God|Et Filium Dei se nominat]], and indeed the natural, only-begotten, consubstantial Son, saying: [[John 10:30|I and the Father are one|Ego et Pater unum sumus]]; and again: [[John 10:29|That which my Father hath given me is greater than all|Pater quod dedit mihi, majus omnibus est]]. Hence again we have in John: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. [[John 5:16|Therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus|Propterea persequebantur Judæi Jesum]], [[John 5:18|because he did not only break the sabbath but also said God was his Father, making himself equal to God|quia non solum solvebat sabbatum, sed et patrem suum dicebat Deum, æqualem se faciens Deo]]. And elsewhere: [[John 10:36|Do you say of him whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the world: Thou blasphemest; because I said: I am the Son of God?|Quem Pater sanctificavit, et misit in mundum, vos dicitis, Quia blasphemas: quia dixi, Filius Dei sum?]]

paras.t: Factus est nobis in traductionem cogitationum nostrarum: id est, non solum reprehendit ac propalavit exteriora nostra peccata, sed etiam secreta vitia cogitationum nostrarum manifestavit: juxta illud, Quum vidisset Jesus cogitationes eorum, dixit. Et alibi habetur: Opus ei non erat ut quis testimonium perhiberet de homine; ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine.
paras.en: [[2:14|He is become a censurer of our thoughts|Factus est nobis in traductionem cogitationum nostrarum]] [*in traductionem*, literally "for an exposing"]: that is, he not only rebuked and laid bare our outward sins, but also made manifest the secret vices of our thoughts: according to that saying, [[Matt 9:4|Jesus seeing their thoughts, said|Quum vidisset Jesus cogitationes eorum, dixit]]. And elsewhere we have: [[John 2:25|he needed not that any should give testimony of man: for he knew what was in man|Opus ei non erat ut quis testimonium perhiberet de homine; ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine]].

paras.t: Gravis est nobis etiam ad videndum, propter rancorem et displicentiam quos contra eum concepimus, quoniam dissimilis est aliis vita illius: quia in omnibus sine personarum acceptione pro veritate zelatur, nec ullum veretur, nec parcit alicui; et immutatæ, id est aliis dissimiles, sunt vitæ ejus, id est actiones, instructiones, institutionesque ejus. Quemadmodum autem similitudo est causa unionis et complacentiæ, sic dissimilitudo aversionem ac displicentiam parit, et veritas odium. Talia tamen sunt scandala passiva et sumpta, non activa et data.
paras.en: [[2:15|He is grievous unto us, even to behold|Gravis est nobis etiam ad videndum]], because of the rancour and dislike we have conceived against him, [[2:15|for his life is not like other men's|quoniam dissimilis est aliis vita illius]]: because in all things, without respect of persons, he is zealous for the truth, and fears no one, and spares no one; [[2:15|and his ways are very different|et immutatæ]], that is, unlike those of others, [[2:15|his ways|sunt vitæ ejus]] [Denis reads *vitæ*, "lives", for the Vulgate's *viæ*, "ways"], that is, his actions, teachings and ordinances. For as likeness is a cause of union and of being well pleased, so unlikeness breeds aversion and dislike, and truth breeds hatred. Yet such are scandals passive and taken, not active and given [that is, offence taken by the ill-disposed, not offence given by the one who acts].

paras.t: Tanquam nugaces, id est vani, fatui et mendaces, æstimati sumus ab illo. Unde loquitur eis in Evangelio: Vos ex patre diabolo estis, et in peccato vestro moriemini. Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit: propterea vos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis. Et rursus: Est Pater meus qui glorificat me: quem vos dicitis quia Deus vester est, et non cognovistis eum. Ego autem novi eum; et si dixero quia non scio eum, ero similis vobis, mendax. Et abstinet se a viis, id est operibus et traditionibus nostris, tanquam ab immunditiis; et præfert novissima justorum, id est, prædicat, laudat, et cunctis præsentibus anteponit finalia bona ac præmia, justis pro mercede præstanda, dicendo: Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum; et rursum, Ibunt justi in vitam æternam; et, Erunt sicut angeli Dei; ac multa similia. Et gloriatur patrem se habere Deum: sicut jam patuit. Et fuit hæc gloriatio sancta et vera, non vana et falsa.
paras.en: [[2:16|as triflers|Tanquam nugaces]], that is, vain, foolish and lying, [[2:16|We are esteemed by him|æstimati sumus ab illo]]. Hence he says to them in the Gospel: [[John 8:44|You are of your father the devil|Vos ex patre diabolo estis]], and [[John 8:21|you shall die in your sin|in peccato vestro moriemini]]. [[John 8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God. Therefore you hear them not, because you are not of God|Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit: propterea vos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis]]. And again: [[John 8:54|It is my Father that glorifieth me, of whom you say that he is your God|Est Pater meus qui glorificat me: quem vos dicitis quia Deus vester est]], [[John 8:55|And you have not known him: but I know him. And if I shall say that I know him not, I shall be like to you, a liar|et non cognovistis eum. Ego autem novi eum; et si dixero quia non scio eum, ero similis vobis, mendax]]. [[2:16|and he abstaineth from our ways|Et abstinet se a viis]], that is, from our works and traditions, [[2:16|as from filthiness|tanquam ab immunditiis]]; [[2:16|and he preferreth the latter end of the just|et præfert novissima justorum]], that is, he preaches, praises and sets before all present things the last goods and rewards to be given to the just as their wages, saying: [[Matt 13:43|shall the just shine as the sun, in the kingdom of their Father|Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum]]; and again: [[Matt 25:46|the just, into life everlasting|Ibunt justi in vitam æternam]]; and: [[Matt 22:30|shall be as the angels of God|Erunt sicut angeli Dei]]; and many like sayings. [[2:16|and glorieth that he hath God for his father|Et gloriatur patrem se habere Deum]]: as has already been shown. And this glorying was holy and true, not vain and false.

paras.t: Videamus ergo, id est, per effectuum evidentiam inquiramus, si, id est an, sermones illius veri sint, et tentemus, id est, experimentaliter scire conemur, quæ ventura sunt illi inter adversa quæ infligeremus ei; et sciemus quæ erunt novissima illius, id est, quæ finaliter ei evenient. Si enim est verus Filius Dei, suscipiet illum, ipsum defendendo et exaudiendo, et liberabit eum de manibus contrariorum, id est inimicorum suorum.
paras.en: [[2:17|Let us see then|Videamus ergo]], that is, let us inquire by the evidence of the outcome, [[2:17|if|si]], that is, whether, [[2:17|his words be true|sermones illius veri sint]], [[2:17|and let us prove|et tentemus]], that is, let us try to know by experience, [[2:17|what shall happen to him|quæ ventura sunt illi]] amid the adversities we should inflict on him [these words, *inter adversa quæ infligeremus ei*, are printed in italics as part of the text, though they are not in the Vulgate]; [[2:17|and we shall know what his end shall be|et sciemus quæ erunt novissima illius]], that is, what will befall him at the last. [[2:18|For if he be the true son of God, he will defend him|Si enim est verus Filius Dei, suscipiet illum]], by defending him and hearing his prayer, [[2:18|and will deliver him from the hands of his enemies|et liberabit eum de manibus contrariorum]], that is, of his foes.

paras.t: Istud, secundum Augustinum, fuit totum acumen Judæorum. Viderunt etenim Jesum multa et præclarissima miracula facientem, et copiosum post se populum deducentem, ac omnium terrenorum prædicantem contemptum. Sicque videbant sibi ab ipso principatum, ad quem maxime anhelabant, auferri. Ideo collegerunt concilium pontifices et Pharisæi, et dicebant: Quid facimus, quia hic homo multa signa facit? Si dimittimus eum sic, omnes credent in eum; et venient Romani, et tollent locum nostrum et gentem. Sicque ex una parte metuebant eum ita dimittere, ex alia quoque parte verebantur eum occidere, tot et tanta agentem prodigia. Ideo invenerunt medium istud, ut per adversa et amarissima supplicia explorarent an vere esset Filius Dei, dicentes: Si verus Filius Dei est, non permittet eum Pater occidi, sed eruet eum de manibus nostris. Quod si fecerit, agnoscemus quod sit Filius Dei, et credemus in eum. Si vero permiserit eum occidi, patebit quod non sit nisi quod ceteri, nec sit verus Filius Patris æterni. Huic demum considerationi B. Augustini concordat evangelica veritas, quoniam Christo in cruce suspenso, dixerunt: Si rex Israel est (vel, Si hic est Christus Dei electus), descendat nunc de cruce, et credimus ei. Insuper, teste Augustino, volebant a morte Christi immunes videri: propter quod tradiderunt eum Pilato, ut morti adjudicaretur ab illo, eis accusantibus tantum. Verumtamen Pilato hoc facere renuente, a propria invidia incitati sunt et coacti, importune crucifixionem ejus efflagitare. Hinc etiam leguntur dixisse Apostolis: Replestis Jerusalem doctrina vestra, et vultis super nos inducere sanguinem hominis istius. Quasi dicant: Nos sumus immunes a sanguine ejus, quem præses per suos crucifixit ministros, et quem tradidit suus discipulus. Iis concordant sequentia.
paras.en: This, according to Augustine, was the whole shrewdness of the Jews. For they saw Jesus working many and most glorious miracles, and drawing a great people after him, and preaching contempt of all earthly things. And so they saw that the rule they most longed for was being taken from them by him. [[John 11:47|The chief priests, therefore, and the Pharisees gathered a council and said: What do we, for this man doth many miracles?|collegerunt concilium pontifices et Pharisæi, et dicebant: Quid facimus, quia hic homo multa signa facit?]] [[John 11:48|If we let him alone so, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come, and take away our place and nation|Si dimittimus eum sic, omnes credent in eum; et venient Romani, et tollent locum nostrum et gentem]]. And so on the one hand they feared to let him alone thus, and on the other they were afraid to kill him, since he was doing so many and such great wonders. Therefore they found this middle way: to search out by adversities and the bitterest torments whether he was truly the Son of God, saying: If he is the true Son of God, the Father will not allow him to be killed, but will rescue him from our hands. If he does so, we shall acknowledge that he is the Son of God, and shall believe in him. But if he allows him to be killed, it will be plain that he is nothing but what the rest are, and not the true Son of the eternal Father. With this consideration of Blessed Augustine the truth of the Gospel agrees, since when Christ was hanging on the cross they said: [[Matt 27:42|If he be the king of Israel|Si rex Israel est]] (or, [[Luke 23:35|if he be Christ, the elect of God|Si hic est Christus Dei electus]]), [[Matt 27:42|let him now come down from the cross: and we will believe him|descendat nunc de cruce, et credimus ei]]. Moreover, as Augustine bears witness, they wished to appear free of Christ's death: for which reason they delivered him to Pilate[[Matt 27:2||]], that he might be condemned to death by him, with themselves only as accusers. But when Pilate refused to do this, they were driven and forced by their own envy to demand his crucifixion importunately[[Matt 27:23||]]. Hence too we read that they said to the Apostles: [[Acts 5:28|you have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine: and you have a mind to bring the blood of this man upon us|Replestis Jerusalem doctrina vestra, et vultis super nos inducere sanguinem hominis istius]]. As if they said: We are free of the blood of him whom the governor crucified by his own servants, and whom his own disciple betrayed. With these things what follows agrees.

paras.t: Contumelia et tormento interrogemus eum: id est, inferendo ei opprobria et tormenta, inquiramus et perscrutemur an sit Filius Dei, et eruendus ex manibus nostris; ut sciamus reverentiam ejus, id est, an vere sit honorandus ut Filius Dei et rex Messias; et probemus patientiam illius, an scilicet impleat opere, quæ alios docuit de patientiæ exhibitione. Morte turpissima condemnemus eum, id est, procuremus eum adjudicari patibulo: quæ fuit turpissima mors in lege, juxta illud Deuteronomii: Maledictus qui pendet in ligno. Quasi dicant: Tam ignominiosissimam mortem Deus Pater nequaquam Filio suo infligi permittet. Ideo subdunt: erit enim ei respectus ex sermonibus illius: id est, ex verbis ejus conspiciemus atque pensabimus quid habeat veritas: quia si poterimus eum exstinguere, cognoscemus quod mendaciter vocavit se Filium Dei.
paras.en: [[2:19|Let us examine him by outrages and tortures|Contumelia et tormento interrogemus eum]]: that is, by bringing reproaches and torments upon him, let us inquire and search out whether he is the Son of God, and is to be rescued out of our hands; [[2:19|that we may know his meekness|ut sciamus reverentiam ejus]] [*reverentiam ejus*, literally "his reverence", which Denis takes as the reverence due to him], that is, whether he is truly to be honoured as the Son of God and the King Messias; [[2:19|and try his patience|et probemus patientiam illius]], that is, whether he fulfils in deed what he taught others about showing patience. [[2:20|Let us condemn him to a most shameful death|Morte turpissima condemnemus eum]], that is, let us bring it about that he is sentenced to the gibbet, which was the most shameful death in the law, according to that saying of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 21:23|accursed of God that hangeth on a tree|Maledictus qui pendet in ligno]]. As if they said: God the Father will never allow so very ignominious a death to be inflicted on his Son. Therefore they add: [[2:20|for there shall be respect had unto him by his words|erit enim ei respectus ex sermonibus illius]] [*respectus*, "a looking at, a regard"]: that is, from his words we shall see and weigh what truth there is in them: for if we are able to put him to death, we shall know that he lyingly called himself the Son of God.

paras.t: Hæc cogitaverunt iniqui præfati, et erraverunt, quum in Prophetis apertissime prænuntiata sit passio Christi. Ideo nullam prorsus consequentiam habuit: Si hic est Christus, descendat de cruce; et, Si filius Dei est, liberabit eum de manu contrariorum. Imo, si non permisisset eum Pater occidi, consequens fuisset quod non fuisset Christus Filius Dei, de quo erat prædictum quod occideretur, et sua passione redimeret mundum. Excæcavit enim illos malitia eorum, id est invidia, impatientia, ira, amaritudo, indignatio, superbia, quas contra Christum conceperant: ita quod quanto plura et majora fecit miracula, quo gloriosius prædicavit, et Christum se esse monstravit, eo plus torquebantur, et omnia interpretabantur in pejus, ac dæmonium principi adscripserunt. Et probabilis illa, quam ante habuerunt ad tempus de Christo, notitia, post passiones istas nequissimas fuit exstincta et offuscata.
paras.en: [[2:21|These things they thought|Hæc cogitaverunt]], these wicked men aforesaid, [[2:21|and were deceived|et erraverunt]], since the passion of Christ was most plainly foretold in the Prophets. Therefore there was no force at all in the reasoning, If this is the Christ, let him come down from the cross[[Matt 27:42||]][[Mark 15:32||]]; and, If he is the Son of God, he [[2:18|will deliver him from the hands of his enemies|liberabit eum de manu contrariorum]]. On the contrary, if the Father had not allowed him to be killed, it would have followed that he was not the Christ, the Son of God, of whom it had been foretold that he would be killed and by his passion redeem the world. [[2:21|for their own malice blinded them|Excæcavit enim illos malitia eorum]], that is, the envy, impatience, anger, bitterness, indignation and pride which they had conceived against Christ: so that the more and the greater the miracles he worked, the more gloriously he preached and showed himself to be the Christ, the more they were tormented, and interpreted everything for the worse, and ascribed it to the prince of devils[[Matt 12:24||]]. And that probable knowledge of Christ which they had had for a time before was, after these most wicked passions, extinguished and darkened.

paras.t: Et nescierunt sacramenta Dei, id est secreta ejus mysteria atque consilia de modo salvandi genus humanum per Christi oblationem; neque mercedem speraverunt justitiæ, id est felicitatem æternam pro actibus justitiæ retribuendam. Certum est enim quod impii isti Judæi non habuerunt spem formatam, quæ ex gratia Dei et actibus bonis procedit. Nec judicaverunt honorem animarum sanctarum: id est, non cognoverunt per fidem formatam, nec discreverunt, quam gloriose coronandæ sint a Deo animæ sanctæ; sed temporalia sola pensabant.
paras.en: [[2:22|And they knew not the secrets of God|Et nescierunt sacramenta Dei]], that is, his hidden mysteries and counsels about the way of saving mankind through the offering of Christ; [[2:22|nor hoped for the wages of justice|neque mercedem speraverunt justitiæ]], that is, the eternal happiness to be paid for acts of justice. For it is certain that these wicked Jews did not have formed hope [that is, hope given life by charity], which proceeds from the grace of God and from good acts. [[2:22|nor esteemed the honour of holy souls|Nec judicaverunt honorem animarum sanctarum]]: that is, they did not know by formed faith [faith given life by charity], nor discern, how gloriously holy souls are to be crowned by God; but they weighed temporal things alone.

paras.t: Quoniam Deus creavit hominem, scilicet primum nostrum parentem Adam, inexterminabilem, id est impassibilem et immortalem, nisi peccaret. Nam animam ejus condidit immortalem, et per originalem justitiam mansisset corpus animæ perfecte subjectum, et a læsionibus liberum. Et ad imaginem similitudinis suæ fecit illum, id est ad imitationem sui ipsius, ut per intellectum, memoriam, voluntatem esset capax Dei, contemplando, amando, ac inhærendo: juxta illud, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram.
paras.en: [[2:23|For God created man|Quoniam Deus creavit hominem]], namely our first parent Adam, [[2:23|incorruptible|inexterminabilem]], that is, incapable of suffering and immortal, unless he should sin. For he made his soul immortal, and through original justice [the state of grace and integrity in which the first man was created] the body would have remained perfectly subject to the soul, and free from harm. [[2:23|and to the image of his own likeness he made him|Et ad imaginem similitudinis suæ fecit illum]], that is, to the imitation of himself, so that through understanding, memory and will he might be capable of God, by contemplating, loving and cleaving to him: according to that saying, [[Gen 1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]].

paras.t: Invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum: id est, diabolus ex invidia, qua invidit primo parenti ac ejus posteritati beatitudinem, quam ipse amiserat, decepit et ad transgressionem induxit primos parentes. Qui mox ob suam transgressionem originali justitia sunt privati: sicque mente eorum per inobedientiam a Deo aversa, statim cœpit sensualitas rationi reniti, et corpus spiritui; sicque corpus necessitati moriendi subjectum est. Itaque mors culpæ, per suggestionem diaboli intravit in primos parentes, et per illam mors corporalis: ac ita in posteros eorumdem, qui originali justitia destituti nascuntur. Imitantur autem illum, id est diabolum, et ejus invidiam atque malitiam, qui sunt ex parte illius, id est reprobi et iniqui, perditionisque filii: quibus dicitur apud Joannem, Vos ex patre diabolo estis.
paras.en: [[2:24|But by the envy of the devil, death came into the world|Invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum]]: that is, the devil, out of the envy with which he envied the first parent and his posterity the beatitude which he himself had lost, deceived our first parents and led them into transgression[[Gen 3:1||]][[Gen 3:13||]] [the margin gives Gen. iii, 1–7, 13]. And at once, for their transgression, they were deprived of original justice: and so, their mind having been turned away from God by disobedience, sensuality at once began to strive against reason, and the body against the spirit; and so the body was made subject to the necessity of dying. Thus the death of guilt entered into our first parents through the suggestion of the devil, and through it bodily death: and so into their descendants, who are born destitute of original justice. [[2:25|And they follow him|Imitantur autem illum]], that is, the devil, and his envy and malice, [[2:25|that are of his side|qui sunt ex parte illius]], that is, the reprobate and wicked, the sons of perdition: to whom it is said in John, [[John 8:44|You are of your father the devil|Vos ex patre diabolo estis]].

paras.t: Insuper, ab illo loco, Circumveniamus ergo justum, quidam exponunt de impiis, et de populo Judæorum olim justo: de quo Scriptura aliquando loquitur quasi de homine uno. Ita quod gentiles adversantes populo illi, dixerunt: Circumveniamus justum, id est populum istum Dei cultorem; quoniam contrarius est operibus nostris, quia idololatriam vitat ac reprobat, et improperat nobis peccata legis, id est vitia quæ contra naturalem facimus legem. Promittit se scientiam Dei habere, scilicet legem desuper datam, et filium Dei se nominat: juxta illud Deuteronomii, Filii estote Domini Dei vestri. Unde et in Exodo Dominus loquitur: Filius meus primogenitus Israel; et in Osee: Puer Israel, et dilexi eum; et ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum. Justi autem dicuntur filii Dei per adoptionem. Factus est nobis in traductionem cogitationum nostrarum: quia Prophetæ, Deo revelante, frequenter noverunt et reprehenderunt cogitationes impiorum gentilium. Gravis est nobis etiam ad videndum: multum enim oderant filios Israel; quoniam dissimilis est aliis vita illius: quia secundum legis præcepta, habuerunt modum vivendi omnino diversum a ritu gentilium. Et juxta expositionem præhabitam, potest littera sequens aliqualiter applicari ad istum sensum; non tamen proprie, ut videtur.
paras.en: Further, from the place [[2:12|Let us, therefore, lie in wait for the just|Circumveniamus ergo justum]], some expound it of the wicked, and of the people of the Jews, once just, of whom Scripture sometimes speaks as of one man. So that the Gentiles, being hostile to that people, said: [[2:12|lie in wait for the just|Circumveniamus justum]], that is, this people that worships God; because [[2:12|he is contrary to our doings|contrarius est operibus nostris]], since it shuns and condemns idolatry, [[2:12|and upbraideth us with transgressions of the law|et improperat nobis peccata legis]], that is, the vices we commit against the natural law. [[2:13|He boasteth that he hath the knowledge of God|Promittit se scientiam Dei habere]], namely the law given from above, [[2:13|and calleth himself the son of God|et filium Dei se nominat]]: according to that saying of Deuteronomy, [[Deut 14:1|Be ye children of the Lord your God|Filii estote Domini Dei vestri]]. Hence also in Exodus the Lord says: [[Ex 4:22|Israel is my son, my firstborn|Filius meus primogenitus Israel]]; and in Osee: [[Osee 11:1|Israel was a child, and I loved him: and I called my son out of Egypt|Puer Israel, et dilexi eum; et ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum]]. And the just are called sons of God by adoption. [[2:14|He is become a censurer of our thoughts|Factus est nobis in traductionem cogitationum nostrarum]]: because the Prophets, by God's revelation, often knew and rebuked the thoughts of the wicked Gentiles. [[2:15|He is grievous unto us, even to behold|Gravis est nobis etiam ad videndum]]: for they greatly hated the children of Israel; [[2:15|for his life is not like other men's|quoniam dissimilis est aliis vita illius]]: because, according to the precepts of the law, they had a way of life altogether different from the rites of the Gentiles. And following the exposition given above, the letter that follows can in some fashion be applied to this sense, though not properly, as it seems.

paras.t: Porro, spiritualiter potest exponi de hæreticis ac aliis perfidis, populum catholicum tanquam Dei filium adoptivum persequentibus. Qui populus vere habet scientiam Dei, et gloriatur se dicere Deo, Pater noster qui es in cœlis; ac infideles reputat prorsus erroneos. Quem dum perfidi et iniqui persequuntur ac superant, præsumunt populum christianum a Deo relictum ac reprobum, ignorantes quod Deus suos electos in hac vita exercet, purgat ac probat per reprobos et injustos. Istas expositiones, brevitati studens, tango solum, non prosequor: quia ex prima jam introducta expositione possunt facillime elici ac patere.
paras.en: Again, spiritually, it can be expounded of heretics and other faithless men who persecute the Catholic people as God's adopted son. This people truly has the knowledge of God, and glories in saying to God, [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster qui es in cœlis]]; and it reckons unbelievers altogether in error. And when the faithless and wicked persecute and overcome it, they presume that the Christian people is forsaken by God and reprobate, not knowing that God exercises, purges and proves his elect in this life through the reprobate and unjust. These expositions, aiming at brevity, I only touch on and do not pursue: for they can very easily be drawn out and made plain from the first exposition already set forth.

3.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI TERTII : JUSTORUM AUTEM ANIMÆ IN MANU DEI SUNT.
3.title_en: Declaration of the third chapter: But the souls of the just are in the hand of God

paras.t: Capitulo præcedenti descriptæ sunt perversitates et opera impiorum, et qualiter circa Christum se habuerunt. Hic describuntur virtutes, actiones, proprietates, privilegia, ac præmia electorum atque Sanctorum, potissime martyrum : quorum constantiam ac martyrium impii reputaverunt insaniam ac perditionem.
paras.en: In the preceding chapter were described the perversities and works of the wicked, and how they behaved towards Christ. Here are described the virtues, actions, properties, privileges and rewards of the elect and of the Saints, above all of the martyrs, whose constancy and martyrdom the wicked reckoned madness and perdition.

paras.t: Justorum autem animæ in manu Dei sunt. Multis modis accipitur manus Dei in Scripturis. Primo, pro omnipotentia ejus : sicque universa creata in manu sunt Dei, juxta illud Psalmi : In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ. Secundo, pro conservatione ipsius : sic quoque omnia in manu Dei exsistunt. Tertio, pro vindicta divinæ justitiæ : juxta illud, Inveniatur manus tua omnibus inimicis tuis. Quarto, pro gratioso et pio auxilio, seu magnifico opere Dei : sicut in Exodo legitur eduxisse filios Israel de Ægypto in manu excelsa. Quinto, pro præsentiali repræsentatione : sicut in Isaia, Ecce in manibus meis descripsi te. Sexto, pro Filio Dei Patris. Nam sicut Spiritus Sanctus dicitur digitus Dei, quia per eum secreta indicat ac revelat, prout in Evangelio loquitur Christus, Si in digito Dei ejicio dæmones; sic Filius dicitur manus, seu dextera ac brachium Patris, quia per Filium omnia operatur. De quo Isaias asserit : Paravit Dominus brachium sanctum suum in oculis omnium gentium. Septimo, pro divina protectione : et ita jam dicitur, Justorum animæ in manu Dei sunt : quia a corpore exeuntes, non pereunt, nec damnantur, ut perfidi putaverunt; sed custodiuntur a Deo, et de sua beatitudine fiunt securæ. Imo sub evangelica lege mox admittuntur ad gloriam animæ martyrum : et ita sunt in manu pietatis divinæ, per assecurationem salutis collatæ. Quæ autem aliquid deferunt secum purgabile, sunt usque ad suæ consummationem purgationis in purgatorii locis : in quibus tamen certæ sunt de adeptione præstandæ salutis. Porro ante Christi passionem, animæ sanctæ nihil secum portantes purgabile, erant in limbo patrum, et de futura gloria erant tutæ : a qua retardabantur ob reatum naturæ, qui auferri non poterat, nisi per Christum.
paras.en: [[3:1|But the souls of the just are in the hand of God|Justorum autem animæ in manu Dei sunt]]. The hand of God is taken in many ways in the Scriptures. First, for his omnipotence: and so all created things are in the hand of God, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 94:4|in his hand are all the ends of the earth|In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ]]. Secondly, for his preserving: so too all things exist in the hand of God. Thirdly, for the vengeance of divine justice, according to that: [[Ps 20:9|Let thy hand be found by all thy enemies|Inveniatur manus tua omnibus inimicis tuis]]. Fourthly, for the gracious and loving help, or the mighty work, of God: as we read in Exodus that he brought the children of Israel out of Egypt [[Ex 14:8|in a mighty hand|in manu excelsa]]. Fifthly, for a representation that keeps a thing present before him: as in Isaias, [[Is 49:16|Behold, I have graven thee in my hands|Ecce in manibus meis descripsi te]]. Sixthly, for the Son of God the Father. For as the Holy Ghost is called the finger of God, because through him God shows and reveals secrets, as Christ says in the Gospel, [[Luke 11:20|if I by the finger of God cast out devils|Si in digito Dei ejicio dæmones]]; so the Son is called the hand, or the right hand and arm, of the Father, because through the Son he works all things. Of him Isaias declares: [[Is 52:10|The Lord hath prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the Gentiles|Paravit Dominus brachium sanctum suum in oculis omnium gentium]]. Seventhly, for divine protection: and it is in this way that it is said here, [[3:1|the souls of the just are in the hand of God|Justorum animæ in manu Dei sunt]]: because on going out from the body they do not perish, nor are they damned, as the faithless thought; but they are kept by God, and are made secure of their beatitude. Indeed, under the law of the Gospel the souls of the martyrs are admitted at once to glory: and so they are in the hand of the divine mercy, through the assurance of salvation bestowed on them. But those that carry with them something to be purged are in the places of purgatory until their purging is complete: yet in those places they are certain of attaining the salvation that is to be granted them. Further, before the passion of Christ, holy souls that carried nothing with them to be purged were in the limbo of the fathers, and were safe as to their future glory: from which they were held back by the guilt of nature [that is, original sin], which could not be taken away except through Christ.

paras.t: Et non tanget illos tormentum mortis, id est pœna æternæ damnationis, quæ est mors secunda ac crudelissima. Unde in Apocalypsi habetur : Pars iniquorum erit in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure, quod est mors secunda. Vel ideo ait, Non tanget illos tormentum mortis, quia tormenta quæ sustinuerunt, non occiderunt eos totaliter : imo principalis pars, scilicet anima, mansit immortalis. Ideo subditur :
paras.en: [[3:1|And the torment of death shall not touch them|Et non tanget illos tormentum mortis]], that is, the pain of eternal damnation, which is the second and most cruel death. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: The portion of the wicked shall be [[Apoc 21:8|in the pool burning with fire and brimstone, which is the second death|in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure, quod est mors secunda]]. Or he says, [[3:1|the torment of death shall not touch them|Non tanget illos tormentum mortis]], because the torments they endured did not kill them wholly: rather the principal part, namely the soul, remained immortal. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Visi sunt oculis insipientium mori : id est, insipientes tyranni et infideles æstimaverunt eos mori, quantum ad corpus et animam, vel damnari in anima; et æstimata est afflictio exitus illorum : id est, impii illi reputaverunt exitum justorum de sæculo isto, videlicet mortem, non esse nisi afflictionem, et non esse januam ad vitam beatam : quia non crediderunt esse vitam aliam post præsentem, aut crediderunt eos post corporalem temporalemque mortem descendere ad infernum in afflictionem acerbiorem. Et ab itinere justo abierunt in exterminium, id est, ipsi insipientes recedentes a via justitiæ, exterminati sunt, et eradicati a statu salutis, a vita naturæ et gratiæ, et in mortem damnationis prolapsi sunt;
paras.en: [[3:2|In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die|Visi sunt oculis insipientium mori]]: that is, the unwise tyrants and unbelievers thought that they died as to body and soul, or that they were damned in the soul; [[3:2|and their departure was taken for misery|et æstimata est afflictio exitus illorum]]: that is, those wicked men reckoned the departure of the just from this world, namely death, to be nothing but misery, and not the gate to the life of bliss: because they did not believe that there is another life after the present one, or else they believed that after bodily and temporal death the just went down to hell, into a sharper misery. And they went away from the just way into destruction [this clause stands in Denis's text, but not in the Clementine Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims], that is, these unwise men themselves, withdrawing from the way of justice, have been destroyed and rooted out from the state of salvation, from the life of nature and of grace, and have fallen into the death of damnation;

paras.t: et quod a nobis est iter exterminii, id est in præfatam exterminationem, quæ est eradicatio seu iter exterminationis a nobis, id est recessus ac defectio ab hac vita. Vel sensus est, quod justi reputatione atque judicio impiorum recesserunt a recto itinere veritatis, in exterminationem. De qua fertur in Isaia, Tollatur impius, ne videat gloriam Dei; et alibi, Exterminati sunt, et ad inferos descenderunt; atque alio loco, Vidi iniquos Domino flante perisse. Illi autem, scilicet justi, sunt in pace æternitatis : quia quantum ad animam, ad quietem pervenerunt perpetuam, et ab inquietudinibus atque laboribus vitæ præsentis requieverunt, prout in Apocalypsi asseritur : Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur; amodo jam dicit Spiritus, ut requiescant a laboribus suis.
paras.en: [[3:3|And their going away from us|et quod a nobis est iter]] [[3:3|for utter destruction|exterminii]] [exterminium, a rooting out or driving out; the Douay-Rheims has utter destruction], that is, was taken for the destruction spoken of above, which is a rooting out; or, the way of destruction from us, that is, the departure and failing from this life. Or the sense is that, in the reckoning and judgement of the wicked, the just went away from the right way of truth into destruction. Of this it is said in Isaias, Let the wicked be taken away, that he may not see the glory of God[[Is 26:10||]] [the margin gives Is. xxvi, 10, according to the Septuagint; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have: he shall not see the glory of the Lord]; and elsewhere, [[Bar 3:19|They are cut off, and are gone down to hell|Exterminati sunt, et ad inferos descenderunt]] [exterminati, the same word as in the verse]; and in another place, I have seen the wicked perish by the blast of the Lord[[Job 4:8||]][[Job 4:9||]] [a free rendering of Job 4:8–9]. [[3:3|But they|Illi autem]], namely the just, [[3:3|are in peace|sunt in pace]] of eternity: because as to the soul they have come to everlasting rest, and have rested from the disquiets and labours of the present life, as is declared in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 14:13|Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth now, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours|Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur; amodo jam dicit Spiritus, ut requiescant a laboribus suis]].

paras.t: Etsi, id est quamvis, coram hominibus, imo et ab impiis ac tyrannis, tormenta passi sunt : juxta illud ad Hebræos : Ludibria et verbera experti, insuper et vincula et carceres; lapidati sunt, secti sunt, tentati sunt, in occisione gladii mortui sunt; spes illorum immortalitate plena est, id est, æternam ac securam salutem est consecuta. Vel : Spes illorum, id est merces sperata ab eis, videlicet salus perpetua, immortalitate plena est, quia in nullo potest deficere, prout apud Isaiam scriptum est : Lætitia sempiterna super capita eorum; gaudium et lætitiam obtinebunt, et fugiet dolor et gemitus.
paras.en: [[3:4|And though|Etsi]], that is, although, [[3:4|in the sight of men|coram hominibus]], nay, even at the hands of the wicked and of tyrants, [[3:4|they suffered torments|tormenta passi sunt]], according to that to the Hebrews: They [[Heb 11:36|had trial of mockeries and stripes: moreover also of bands and prisons|Ludibria et verbera experti, insuper et vincula et carceres]]; [[Heb 11:37|They were stoned, they were cut asunder, they were tempted, they were put to death by the sword|lapidati sunt, secti sunt, tentati sunt, in occisione gladii mortui sunt]]; [[3:4|their hope is full of immortality|spes illorum immortalitate plena est]], that is, has attained eternal and secure salvation. Or: [[3:4|their hope|Spes illorum]], that is, the reward hoped for by them, namely everlasting salvation, [[3:4|is full of immortality|immortalitate plena est]], because it can fail in nothing, as it is written in Isaias: [[Is 51:11|joy everlasting shall be upon their heads, they shall obtain joy and gladness, sorrow and mourning shall flee away|Lætitia sempiterna super capita eorum; gaudium et lætitiam obtinebunt, et fugiet dolor et gemitus]].

paras.t: In paucis vexati corporaliter, id est, parva et modica passi tormenta, comparatione æternæ et ineffabilis felicitatis. Propter quod loquitur Paulus : Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam; itemque, Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis. Vel, In paucis, id est corporalibus, vexati : quæ communia sunt hominibus ac jumentis, et respectu spiritualium, præsertim bonorum cœlestis patriæ, pauca sunt, sicut in Evangelio dicitur servo fideli : Quia super pauca fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam. In multis bene disponentur, id est, copiosa præmia consequentur, atque in anima et corpore glorificabuntur, sicut Paulus et Isaias testantur, quod oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quæ præparavit Deus his qui diligunt eum. Unde Christus dixit in Cœna novissima : Ego dispono vobis regnum; et rursus, Vado parare vobis locum.
paras.en: [[3:5|Afflicted in few things|In paucis vexati]] in body, that is, having suffered small and slight torments in comparison with eternal and unspeakable happiness. For which reason Paul says: [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam]]; and again, [[2 Cor 4:17|that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation|Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ]] [[2 Cor 4:17|worketh for us|operatur in nobis]] [[2 Cor 4:17|an eternal weight of glory|æternum gloriæ pondus]]. Or: [[3:5|in few things|In paucis]], that is, in bodily things, [[3:5|afflicted|vexati]]: things which are common to men and beasts, and which are few in respect of spiritual things, above all of the goods of the heavenly fatherland: as it is said in the Gospel to the faithful servant: [[Matt 25:21|because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will place thee over many things|Quia super pauca fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam]][[Matt 25:23||]]. [[3:5|In many they shall be well rewarded|In multis bene disponentur]] [disponentur, literally 'shall be well disposed', that is, set in order; hence Christ's I dispose to you a kingdom, below], that is, they shall obtain abundant rewards, and shall be glorified in soul and body, as Paul and Isaias testify, [[1 Cor 2:9|That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard: neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him|quod oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quæ præparavit Deus his qui diligunt eum]][[Is 64:4||]]. Hence Christ said at the Last Supper: [[Luke 22:29|I dispose to you|Ego dispono vobis]] [[Luke 22:29|a kingdom|regnum]]; and again, [[John 14:2|I go to prepare a place for you|Vado parare vobis locum]].

paras.t: Quoniam Deus tentavit eos. Jacobus apostolus ait : Nemo, quum tentatur, dicat quoniam a Deo tentatur; Deus enim neminem tentat. Quomodo ergo nunc dicitur, Deus tentavit eos? Et respondendum, quod multiplex est tentatio : Una, quæ ordinatur ad fallendum atque nocendum : et sic tentat diabolus. Alia, quæ ordinatur ad sumendum experimentum de re incognita : sicque homines aliquando tentant. Alia, quæ ordinatur ad exercitationem et profectum tentati, et ad informationem ædificationemque aliorum : et sic Deus tentat electos ac virtuosos, sicut tentavit Abraham, Job et Tobiam. Unde et Moyses monet : Recordaberis cuncti itineris, per quod adduxit te Dominus, ut affligeret te atque tentaret. Itaque, Deus tentavit eos, id est, per adversa exercitavit, approbavit, purgavit, et aliis manifestavit illos. Et invenit illos dignos se, id est sua beatifica visione, in quantum ex caritate omnia æquanimiter pertulerunt ad gloriam Dei, Spiritu Sancto actualiter concurrente et movente interius ad taliter patiendum. Sic enim principium effectivum meritorii actus, fuit correspondens et proportionatum fini retributionis beatæ, id est beatificæ visioni seu ejus objecto. Nec obstat illud Apostoli, Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam : quia afflictiones vitæ præsentis secundum se consideratæ, non sunt condignæ gloria tanta; sed consideratæ modo prætacto, cum caritatis et divinæ motionis inclusione, sunt dignæ. Nam et idem Apostolus alibi exhortatur : Ut ambuletis digne Deo.
paras.en: [[3:5|Because God hath tried them|Quoniam Deus tentavit eos]] [tentavit, 'tempted' as well as 'tried'; hence the difficulty that follows]. The apostle James says: [[Jas 1:13|Let no man, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God|Nemo, quum tentatur, dicat quoniam a Deo tentatur]]; for God [[Jas 1:13|tempteth no man|neminem tentat]]. How then is it said here, [[3:5|God hath tried them|Deus tentavit eos]]? The answer is that temptation is of many kinds. One is ordered to deceiving and harming: and so the devil tempts. Another is ordered to making trial of a thing not known: and so men sometimes tempt. Another is ordered to the exercise and progress of the one tempted, and to the instruction and edification of others: and so God tempts the elect and the virtuous, as he tempted Abraham, Job and Tobias. Hence Moses too warns: [[Deut 8:2|thou shalt remember all the way through which the Lord thy God hath brought thee|Recordaberis cuncti itineris, per quod adduxit te Dominus]], [[Deut 8:2|to afflict thee and to prove thee|ut affligeret te atque tentaret]] [tentaret, the word rendered tried in the verse]. So, [[3:5|God hath tried them|Deus tentavit eos]], that is, he exercised them by adversity, approved them, purged them, and showed them forth to others. [[3:5|And found them worthy of himself|Et invenit illos dignos se]], that is, of his beatific vision, inasmuch as out of charity they bore all things with an even mind for the glory of God, the Holy Ghost actually concurring and moving them inwardly to suffer in such a way. For so the effective principle of the meritorious act was answerable and proportioned to the end, the blessed reward, that is, to the beatific vision or to its object. Nor does that saying of the Apostle stand in the way, [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam]]: for the afflictions of the present life considered in themselves are not worthy of so great a glory; but considered in the manner just touched on, as including charity and the divine moving, they are worthy. For the same Apostle elsewhere exhorts: [[1 Thess 2:12|that you would walk worthy of God|Ut ambuletis digne Deo]].

paras.t: Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit illos : id est, sicut aurum in igne fornacis examinatur, an sit verum et bonum aurum, et ibidem ab admixta fæculentia expurgatur, splendidiusque efficitur; sic Deus suos electos in igne adversitatis probavit, et probatos monstravit, puriores effecit, et ad splendorem salutis æternæ perduxit : et quamvis quorumdam corpora combusta sint igne, aut bestiis devorata, animæ tamen majori gratia et gloria sunt dotatæ.
